text: Jesus declares that he is the true vine and his Father the vinedresser, removing every fruitless branch and pruning every fruitful one to bear more.

Jesus charges his disciples to abide in him as the branch in the vine. He is the vine, they are the branches, and whoever abides in him bears much fruit. Apart from him they can do nothing, and branches that do not abide are burned.
Jesus promises that those abiding in him with his words may ask what they wish; the Father is glorified by their fruit.
Jesus tells his disciples that if they love him they will keep his commandments.

Jesus promises that whoever loves him keeps his word and is loved by the Father; he and the Father will come and make their home with him. The word they hear is not his own but the Father's who sent him.
Jesus tells his disciples that they are already clean through the word he has spoken to them.
Jesus says that as the Father has loved him so he has loved them, and bids them abide in his love by keeping his commandments.
Jesus says he has spoken these things to his disciples so that his joy may remain in them and their joy may be full.

subcat: Prayer for Himself — The Hour Has Come
text: Jesus prays the hour has come; he asks the Father to glorify the Son, who has authority to give eternal life to all given him.

subcat: Prayer for Himself — The Hour Has Come
text: Jesus prays that eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent.

subcat: Prayer for Himself — The Hour Has Come
text: Jesus tells the Father he has finished his work, and asks to be glorified with the glory he had with him before the world was.

Jesus prays not for the world but for those the Father has given him, asking the Holy Father to keep them in his name that they may be one as he and the Father are one, and to keep them from the evil one.
Jesus tells the Father the disciples have received the words he gave them, knowing he came from the Father and believing the Father sent him.
Jesus declares to the Father that all his are the Father's and all the Father's are his, and that he is glorified in them.

Jesus tells the Father that he kept the disciples in his name and none was lost but the son of perdition. He speaks these things so they may have his joy, though the world hates them since they are not of the world.
Jesus says that his disciples are not of the world, even as he is not of the world.

Jesus prays that the Father sanctify the disciples through his truth, his word being truth. As the Father sent him into the world he sends them, and for their sakes he sanctifies himself that they also may be sanctified through the truth.

Jesus prays for all who will believe on him through their word, that they all may be one as the Father is in him and he in the Father, so the world may believe the Father sent him and loved them as he loved him.

Jesus tells the Father he has given the disciples the glory given him. He wills that they be with him to behold his glory given before the foundation of the world, so the Father's love for him may be in them, and he in them.
Jesus calls on the righteous Father, saying the world has not known him. But he has, and these know the Father sent him.

Jesus names the first and great commandment as to love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and mind, names love of neighbor as the second like it, and declares that on these two hang all the Law and the Prophets.

Jesus says to love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat and persecute you, calling his hearers to be merciful as their Father is merciful.
Jesus asks what reward there is in loving only those who love you or greeting only your brothers, since even tax collectors do the same, and charges his hearers to lend hoping for nothing in return.
Jesus gives a new commandment, that his disciples love one another as he has loved them, and says by this all will know they are his disciples, if they have love for one another.
Jesus declares no greater love exists than to lay down his life for his friends, and calls them friends if they do what he commands.
Jesus tells his disciples he no longer calls them servants but friends, having made known all he heard from his Father.
Jesus tells his disciples they are the salt of the earth, and that if the salt loses its savor it is good for nothing but to be cast out and trampled under foot.
Jesus tells his hearers they are the light of the world, that a city set on a hill cannot be hidden, and charges them to let their light shine before men so others may glorify their Father in heaven.

Jesus declares he has not come to destroy the law but to fulfill it. Not one jot or tittle will pass till all is fulfilled; whoever breaks the least commandment will be called least, while whoever keeps and teaches them will be great.
Jesus says that unless his hearers' righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, they will in no way enter the kingdom of heaven.

subcat: The Antitheses — “You Have Heard… But I Say to You”
text: Jesus teaches that whoever is angry with his brother without cause is in danger of judgment, and contempt brings one into hell fire.

subcat: The Antitheses — “You Have Heard… But I Say to You”
text: Jesus teaches that whoever looks at a woman to lust has already committed adultery with her in his heart, and if the right eye or hand causes sin, it is better to lose it than have the whole body cast into hell.

subcat: The Antitheses — “You Have Heard… But I Say to You”
text: Jesus says that whoever puts away his wife, except for the cause of fornication, causes her to commit adultery, and whoever marries her who is divorced commits adultery.

subcat: The Antitheses — “You Have Heard… But I Say to You”
text: Jesus charges his hearers not to swear at all, neither by heaven nor earth nor Jerusalem nor their head. Let their yes be yes and their no be no, for whatever is more comes of evil.

subcat: The Antitheses — “You Have Heard… But I Say to You”
text: Jesus teaches his hearers not to resist evil but to turn the other cheek and give their cloak to whoever sues for their coat. He charges them to go two miles with whoever compels them one, and to give to whoever asks.

Jesus warns his hearers not to do their alms before men like the hypocrites who sound a trumpet and already have their reward. Give so secretly the left hand knows not what the right does, and the Father who sees in secret will reward you.

Jesus charges his hearers, when they fast, not to look sad like the hypocrites who disfigure their faces to be seen by men. Let them anoint the head and wash the face so the fast is seen only by the Father, who will reward them.

Jesus says, Judge not, that you be not judged, for the measure you use will be measured back. He asks why they see the speck in their brother's eye but not the beam in their own, charging them first to cast out their own beam.
Jesus charges his hearers not to give what is holy to dogs nor cast pearls before swine, lest they be trampled and turned upon.
Jesus tells the accusers of the woman caught in adultery that he who is without sin among them should cast the first stone at her.

subcat: The Golden Rule and Two Ways
text: Jesus teaches that whatever his hearers would have men do to them, they should do likewise, for this is the law and the prophets.

subcat: The Nature of Greatness in the Kingdom
text: Jesus declares that whoever receives one such little child in his name receives him.

subcat: The Nature of Greatness in the Kingdom
text: Jesus says that many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.

subcat: The Nature of Greatness in the Kingdom
text: Jesus tells the mother of Zebedee's sons and the disciples that they do not know what they ask, that drinking his cup is theirs but sitting at his right or left is the Father's to give. He charges that unlike Gentile rulers who lord it over others, whoever would be great among them must be their servant and whoever would be first must be slave of all.

subcat: The Nature of Greatness in the Kingdom
text: Jesus declares that the greatest among them will be their servant, and that whoever exalts himself will be humbled while whoever humbles himself will be exalted.
Jesus says the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.
Jesus tells Peter he does not understand now but will know later, and unless Peter is washed he has no part with him.
Jesus says one who is washed needs only to wash his feet but is wholly clean, and the disciples are clean, though not all.
Jesus asks the disciples if they know what he has done, and affirms they rightly call him Master and Lord, for so he is.

Jesus tells the disciples that since he their Lord has washed their feet, they ought to wash one another's feet by his example. The servant is not greater than his lord, and they are blessed if they do these things.

Jesus declares that unless his hearers are converted and become as little children they will not enter the kingdom of heaven, and whoever humbles himself as a little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.
Jesus asks the chief priests and scribes if they have never read that out of the mouth of babes and infants God has perfected praise.

subcat: The Power and Accountability of Words
text: Jesus says people will give account for every idle word on judgment day — by their words they will be justified or condemned.

subcat: The Power and Accountability of Words
text: Jesus teaches that what proceeds out of the mouth comes from the heart, and these things defile the person.

Jesus declares his testimony of himself is true because he knows where he came from and where he is going. The law accepts the testimony of two witnesses — he bears witness of himself, and the Father who sent him also bears witness.
Jesus says you will know the truth and the truth will make you free; if the Son makes you free, you are free indeed.
Jesus declares that he is the way, the truth, and the life, and no one comes to the Father except through him.
Jesus repeats his summons that he who has ears to hear, let him hear, calling his hearers throughout his ministry to give spiritual attention to his words.

Jesus tells the disciples it is given them to know the mysteries of the kingdom, and he speaks to the multitudes in parables because seeing they do not see and hearing they do not hear. He blesses their eyes and ears for what they see.
Jesus calls the multitude to him and charges them to hear and understand.
Jesus asks his disciples whether they are also without understanding, that whatever enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled.
Jesus charges his hearers to take heed what they hear, for the measure they use will be measured to them. To him who has, more will be given; from him who has not, even what he has will be taken.
Jesus declares that if any man has ears to hear, let him hear.
Jesus says to let the Pharisees alone, for they are blind leaders of the blind, and if the blind lead the blind both will fall into the ditch.
Jesus tells the Pharisees and Sadducees that when it is evening they say it will be fair weather, for the sky is red.
Jesus asks why this generation seeks a sign, and declares that truly no sign will be given to this generation.
Jesus charges his disciples to take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the leaven of Herod.

Jesus rebukes the disciples for reasoning that they have no bread, asking whether they still do not perceive or understand. He reminds them of the baskets gathered after the five loaves and the seven, asking how they still do not understand.
Jesus says when a cloud rises in the west they predict a shower, and when the south wind blows they predict heat.
Jesus declares he came for judgment, that those who do not see may see and those who see may be made blind.
Jesus tells the Pharisees that if they were blind they would have no sin, but because they say they see, their sin remains.

Jesus warns of false prophets in sheep's clothing who inwardly are ravening wolves. They will be known by their fruits, for a corrupt tree cannot bear good fruit, and every barren tree is hewn down and burned.
Jesus teaches that the tree is known by its fruit. He calls his hearers a generation of vipers, asking how being evil they can speak good, for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.
Jesus charges his disciples to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.

Jesus warns that if anyone says here is Christ or there, they are not to believe it. False christs and false prophets will arise and show great signs and wonders to deceive, if possible, even the elect.

Jesus declares that this is the condemnation: light has come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light because their deeds were evil. Everyone who does evil hates the light, but he who does truth comes to the light.

Jesus tells his disciples not to fear, for there is nothing covered that will not be revealed, nothing hidden that will not be known. What he tells them in darkness, speak in light; what they hear in the ear, preach on the housetops.

Jesus asks whether a candle is brought to be put under a bushel or a bed rather than on a candlestick, declaring that nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor kept secret but that it should come abroad.

Jesus declares to a paralytic that his sins are forgiven, and when scribes call it blasphemy he asks whether it is easier to say your sins are forgiven or to say arise and walk, then heals the man so they may know the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins.
Jesus declares that the woman's many sins are forgiven because she loved much, and the one forgiven little loves little.
Jesus teaches that if you forgive others their trespasses, the heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive, neither will the Father forgive your trespasses.
Jesus answers Peter that he is to forgive a brother not seven times but seventy times seven.
Jesus warns that if you do not forgive, neither will your Father in heaven forgive your trespasses.
Jesus charges that if you bring a gift to the altar and remember a brother has something against you, first be reconciled, then offer it.

Jesus counsels his hearers to agree with their adversary quickly while on the way. Otherwise the adversary will deliver them to the judge and the judge to the officer, and they will be cast into prison until they have paid the last farthing.

Jesus instructs that if a brother trespasses, go and tell him his fault privately. If he refuses, take one or two witnesses. If he still refuses, tell the church; if he refuses the church, let him be as a heathen and a publican.
Jesus declares that whoever divorces his wife, except for fornication, causes her to commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.

Jesus says that God made them male and female, that the two will be one flesh, and what God has joined together let no one separate. Moses permitted divorce only because of hardness of heart, but from the beginning it was not so.

Jesus says not all can receive this saying, only those to whom it is given. He names eunuchs born so, eunuchs made by men, and those who made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven, and bids him who can receive it to receive it.

Jesus tells the Sadducees they err, not knowing the scriptures nor the power of God, that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage but are as the angels of God in heaven, and that God is not the God of the dead but of the living, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Jesus teaches that out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, and blasphemies.

Jesus says he came not to send peace on earth but a sword, to set a man against his father, daughter against mother, and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law, and a man's foes will be those of his own household.
Jesus declares that he who loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him, and he who loves son or daughter more than him is not worthy of him.
refs: Matt 10:37; Matt 15:4; Mark 7:10; Mark 10:19; Luke 18:20; Matt 19:17–19

text: Jesus asks who is his mother and his brothers, then looks at those sitting around him and names them as his mother and his brothers.
Jesus names his mother and his brothers as those who hear the word of God and do it.

Jesus warns that whoever offends one of these little ones would be better off drowned with a millstone around his neck. He charges his hearers not to despise these little ones, whose angels always behold his Father's face.
Jesus bids his disciples let the little children come to him and not forbid them, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.

Jesus teaches his hearers not to lay up treasures on earth where moth and rust corrupt and thieves steal, but to lay up treasures in heaven, for where their treasure is there will their heart be also.

Jesus says the eye is the lamp of the body: if your eye is clear your whole body is full of light, but if your eye is bad your body is full of darkness. How great that darkness, if the light in you is dark.
Jesus declares no one can serve two masters — they will love one and hate the other; you cannot serve God and mammon.
Jesus refuses to arbitrate an inheritance dispute between two brothers, asking who made him a judge or a divider over them.

Jesus says a rich man will hardly enter the kingdom of heaven, for it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. What is impossible with men is possible with God.
Jesus pronounces woe on the rich who have their consolation, and on those full and laughing now, for they will hunger, mourn, and weep.
Jesus charges his hearers to give to the one who asks and not to turn away from the one who would borrow.
Jesus tells the rich young ruler that if he would be perfect he should sell what he has and give to the poor, and he will have treasure in heaven, and come and follow him.

Asked whether it is lawful to give tribute to Caesar, Jesus calls his questioners hypocrites and asks for the tribute coin. Seeing Caesar's image and inscription, he tells them to render to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's.
Jesus says the poor widow has cast more into the treasury than all the others, for they gave out of their abundance but she out of her poverty cast in all she had, even all her living.

Jesus tells of a rich man clothed in purple who fared sumptuously, and a beggar named Lazarus laid at his gate full of sores. When both died, Lazarus was carried into Abraham's bosom while the rich man in hell lifted his eyes in torment. Abraham tells him he received good things in life and Lazarus evil; now Lazarus is comforted, he tormented, and a great gulf is fixed between them.
Jesus, in Abraham's words, declares if they do not hear Moses and the prophets, they will not be persuaded though one rose from the dead.
